subtopic: MR. HALES-ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
MR. HALES-ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. In view of the fact that all of us in this house expect full, complete and correct answers to our questions, be they oral or written, I should like to bring to the attention of the house, the Prime Minister and his parliamentary secretary that I asked a written question to which I received an answer on Monday. Part of the question was:
Who are the auditors for the Company of Young Canadians and what yearly audit fees have been paid?
The answer to that part of my question was
The Auditor General. No fees are charged.
That is completely wrong because, as I recall, the act did not stipulate that the Auditor General would be the auditor, but that the Governor in Council would appoint an auditor for this organization. To the best of my knowledge no auditor has yet been appointed. I have brought this situation to the attention of the house because I feel we should receive full and correct answers.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. J. Benson (Minister of National Revenue and President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: MR. HALES-ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in order to clarify this matter-and I am very sorry if my hon. friend thinks he has been misled in any way-let me say that during the current year payments on behalf of the Company of Young Canadians have been made through the comptroller of the treasury. As a result all these expenditures come under the scrutiny of the Auditor General. In succeeding years it will be necessary for the cabinet to appoint an auditor as provided in the legislation. In respect of the current year the answer given is quite correct.

subtopic: DATES OF VISIT BY HER MAJESTY AND DUKE OF EDINBURGH

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: DATES OF VISIT BY HER MAJESTY AND DUKE OF EDINBURGH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it will be recalled that on September 13 last it was announced from Government House that Her Majesty the Queen and His Royal Highness the Duke of Edinburgh had accepted an invitation of the government of Canada to attend ceremonies in our national capital, celebrating the 100th anniversary of confederation.
I am happy to be able to state now that the dates of the visit of Her Majesty and His Royal Highness have been confirmed. They will arrive at Uplands airport in the late afternoon of Thursday, June 29, and will remain in Canada until late in the evening of Wednesday, July 5. Her Majesty and His Royal Highness, on this occasion, will visit the national capital and will have one day, July 3, at Expo '67.
Her Majesty will address members of both houses of parliament assembled on the anniversary of confederation, Saturday, July 1

February 1, 1967
Impending Royal Visit 1967 at which time the Speakers of the Senate and the House of Commons will each present a loyal address to Her Majesty.
Following these addresses Her Majesty will deliver a special centennial address. Later on July 1 a reception will be held for members of both houses of parliament and their wives at which Her Majesty will attend.
Other details of the program for the royal visit are now being worked out and will be announced in due course from the office of the commissioner general for visits of state. I felt that I should make an announcement of plans for this meeting in the national capital at this time, so that members of parliament and senators may make their plans accordingly.

subtopic: CLAIMS BY CANADIANS AGAINST POLISH GOVERNMENT
CLAIMS BY CANADIANS AGAINST POLISH GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
1.	What is the nature of claims made by Canadians against the Polish government, as a result of nationalizations?
2.	Since when have negotiations on this matter been carried on with the Polish government?
3.	What are the names of the Canadians involved in these claims?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CLAIMS BY CANADIANS AGAINST POLISH GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
1. The claims of Canadians against the Polish government which are registered with the Department of External Affairs are, generally speaking, in respect of property in Poland which was expropriated or otherwise taken without compensation by the Polish authorities after World War II. The claims arose out of the nationalization of

February 1, 1967
Questions
urban residential property, farmland, industries, and other property. According to a well-established principle of international law, the Canadian government advances those claims which belonged to Canadian citizens at the time of loss and continuously thereafter until the presentation of the claim to the Polish authorities.
2.	Within three years after the end of World War II, the Canadian government approached the Polish government with a view to reaching a settlement of nationalization claims of Canadian citizens. However, although this question was reviewed periodically, no basis for progress was found until 1965 when an understanding was reached whereby the Polish authorities agreed to enter into negotiations toward a lump-sum settlement of Canadian claims on the basis of principles similar to those applied in settlements which Poland has concluded with other countries. The Department of External Affairs issued a public announcement on September 1, 1965, inviting Canadians to submit their claims against Poland to this department before January 1, 1966. This deadline was subsequently extended to May 1, 1966. These claims are now being examined in the Department of External Affairs in preparation for negotiations with the Polish authorities. The Secretary of State for External Affairs, upon his return from an official visit to Poland among other countries, stated in the House on November 17, 1966, that "the Polish government is desirous of settling the long-standing matter of the claims of certain Canadians arising out of post-war nationalizations, and in the very near future we expect to enter into detailed negotiations to that end".
3.	The Department of External Affairs had on record, as of January 26, 1967, 562 claims against Poland. Some of these claims are not eligible for espousal by the Canadian government because the requirements of the rule of continuous nationality (see part 1) have not been met. In other cases, the claim may not be espousable because there is no evidence of loss or because the Polish government is not responsible in international law for the loss as, for example, where the loss occurred as a result of a general devaluation of the currency.
It is not usual practice to reveal the names of registered claimants prior to inter-govem-mental claims negotiations.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall start with a stock phrase: another day, another speech.
At the outset of my remarks, I thought of pointing out that since the beginning of this debate on the unification of the armed forces most speakers have noticeably dealt with the subject with much restraint and objectivity and that everyone has put forward ideas that I find, constructive even though I do not approve them all. I am taking the liberty just the same, in spite of fairly recent events, of passing this remark and congratulating the members of the opposition on their participation in this debate.
On the other hand, I must attempt, in a general way, to restate the theory they have set forth. It seems to me that most Conservative members feel they are in favour of a status quo, that is, they accept and even endorse integration, but they wish to stop its progress at this point. I think my friends opposite will find that I am explaining their thinking correctly in saying that.
They are in favour of the status quo. Consequently, the status quo means that they are for integration, but against unification.
On this side of the house, we claim that integration and unification are simply different stages of the same operation. We advance from integration to unification, which is a logical consequence of integration. This attitude could naturally be expressed by a joke which has been made on the subject and, with all due respect for my hon. friends opposite, I should like to recall it. On the basis of comparison, it was said that they are in favour of conception, but against motherhood. Yet, one follows the other. It seems to me, in any case, that some things are being overlooked in all this quesbon of integration and unification of 23033-793
National Defence Act Amendment the forces, when the status quo or even, in some cases, backtracking in being urged. My esteemed friend for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness) waxed nostalgic, the other night, over the three former services. I cannot blame him, but I noted that he was nostalgic over the services at a time when all of them were divided and operated separately, except on occasion, when they might come together, and I said to myself: We are no longer involved in ntegration, we are backtrack ng.
There is nevertheless a fact that must be taken into account, Mr. Speaker. It is that the government has some responsibilities. Everything is changing these days, and it certainly is not the time, in an area as significant and mportant as national defence, to ask the government to advance in every area except in the area of defence. And among the various responsibilities of government, one of them is to ensure that Canada continues along the road to Deace and prosperity. Any nation, large or small, cannot negate the vital task of keeping abreast of the progression of new ideas.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
Indeed, the government would be shirking its responsibilities to the nation and to the people if it did not incorporate new ideas and new ventures which generally can provide our citizens with a better life and better opportunities.
In the field of defence, this government seemingly is providing a force structure which will enable Canada to maintain its sovereignty, which is of course the first objective, and at the same time to make its contribution toward the maintenance of international peace and the deterrence of war. In so doing, we in government would be neglecting our responsibilities to the nation if we did not ensure that the very large portion of money allotted to defence will be spent in a manner which will give our forces the proper equipment they require to support our national and international objectives.
I am convinced we can do this and at the same time generate savings. I feel that the government is more than living up to its responsibilities, to its mandate, in this regard.
As we look at the world we live in, we find ourselves in an era of advanced technology where the armed forces of countries both large and small, possess greater fire power than ever before. We find ourselves in a world whereby fire power has increased so much that we in turn must increase the protection for our troops in the field. We find
February 1, 1967

National Defence Act Amendment ourselves in a mechanized world of armoured personnel carriers, ships that can wash themselves of nuclear fall-out, and self-propelled howitzers which carry their own armoured protection.
We live also in a world of instant communication, of orbiting satellites, tactical communications and radio facilities which can reach any part of the world almost instantly. Thus we live in a world of mobility where long-range heavy transports can fly troops and equipment to the most remote parts of the world at a moment's notice; where helicopters can carry troops to the front lines of battle; where very short take-off tactical fighters and transports have all become part of the armed forces inventory.
Realizing this, it is obvious that no country can be insular. No country can stand alone in the world and say-we are not a part of the international community or we are not affected by the events of the world. And because of all these things, it is clear that each brush fire war which now occurs, has the inherent, potential danger of escalating to an international conflagation. Every armed dispute between any nations must be viewed as one which has a potential danger of disrupting international stability, thereby endangering national security.
We are all aware of these dangers and we are also aware that even the large stable alliances such as NATO must be designed, not only toward stopping a major assault, but also toward stopping minor conflagrations which may break out on any flank. Recognizing this, Canada undertook to provide to the Supreme Commander of NATO, a 1000 man force to the ACE Mobile Force in Europe. It is in this sort of contribution that Canada recognizes her international responsibilities and fulfils her desire and her intention toward maintaining international stability and the deterrence of war.
With these responsibilities in mind, there are a number of options that were available to Canada in the early '60s. We could, for example, contribute all our forces toward the maintenance of peace by placing our forces under the United Nations. As someone has said

"We could put all our eggs in the peacekeeping basket."
The second option open to us was to commit all our forces to the deterrence of war by making additional contributions to NATO and to NORAD and by building up our nuclear capability beyond all reasonable and even logical requirements.


The third option was to keep only enough forces that we would require to maintain our national sovereignty.
Let us examine these three options. If we committed all our forces to the United Nations, then it seems to me we would have to depend upon the United Nations to maintain our national sovereignty, but since the United Nations has neither the military structure nor the forces currently available to undertake such a task, we would be neglecting our responsibilities to the nation and our role which is precisely to maintain national sovereignty.
If we committed all our forces to the deterrence of war in such organizations as NATO and NORAD, we would be neglecting our international responsibilities to the United Nations by not having the forces available for United Nations peacekeeping and peace-restoring actions.
If we undertook the third option of only keeping forces to maintain our national sovereignty, we would place ourselves in an impossible insular position and we would not be living up to our international responsibilities. To put it in very frank terms, we would be saying-"I'm alright Jack, and the rest of the world be damned". That would not be living up to our international responsibilities in the family of nations.
Thus we come to a fourth option. This is the option we have taken. This is the option which permits us to create a proper mix of forces which can be used to contribute to international peacekeeping, which can be used to contribute to the deterrence of war and which can be used to maintain our national sovereignty. This, to me, is the only logical option available to a country of our size, with our population and with our resources. With due respect to those who would suggest that we should take one of the other options, I would simply say that I do not think that the greatest number of Canadians would agree with you.
The Canadian choice of the option that I have just described has been taken because we possess the advanced technology required by our forces to engage in the deterrence of war. The Canadian choice has been taken because we have the resources and the manpower which permit us to accept this proper mix of forces. The Canadian choice for this option has been taken because we are able to produce or procure the necessary equipment for our forces to participate in these various types of conflict.

Above all, however, the Canadian choice of these options has been taken because as good neighbours to all nations, we wish to make our contribution to international stability. For all these reasons, we firmly believe that our choice of these options is not only the right choice but the only choice. I think that Canadians have a sense of pride in the members of our armed forces who are doing their job in NATO, NORAD, in the United Nations and in every part of the world where Canadians are making a contribution to international peace and to the deterrence of war.
Mr. Speaker, there has been a great deal of discussion by members of the opposition regarding our force structure. From what I can gather, and they expressed opinions which in some cases are contradictory, I understand they would have us create a separate force for UN duties; another force for NATO; yet another force to maintain national sovereignty and possibly another force to keep at home for riots, insurrections or what have you. This would be simple, but, I submit, very, very expensive. In fact, Mr. Speaker, it would be a waste of manpower and money.
What we have done and, what I suggest the members of the opposition conveniently ignored, is to create a functional command structure which permits us the flexibility to assign portions of one force to these commitments as the conditions and occasions require. This, in my opinion, is making the maximum effective use of our manpower, equipment and financial resources.
Look at it this way. We have made our choice of options. This choice includes contribution to the deterrence of war; the maintenance of peace, the continuance of national sovereignty and aid to the civil government for internal stability. In all the range of possibilities, there is only one case which comes to mind in which our force structure could not possibly operate. That case would have to include an outbreak of major war in Europe plus many UN peacekeeping operations in separate parts of the world, plus a direct enemy land/sea and air attack on Canada and finally insurrections in all the major Canadian centres. This is what the opposition wants us to prepare for, but I submit in such a case, Mr. Speaker, I doubt very much if any force structure we created would withstand the test. In fact what I am describing is total world anarchy-something which none of us realistically expect to happen.
On the other hand, it would be incomprehensible to have forces which are only 23033-793J
National Defence Act Amendment trained and equipped to fight a nuclear war committed to UN peace restoring action or to restore civil order elsewhere. Now, I admit that there are the two extremes, but between these extremes we are committed to provide a force, or portions of a force, depending on the requirements.
This is the crux of the problem. From a single force containing land, sea and air elements, we must be in a position where we can detach the required portions necessary to fulfil a particular commitment. If the particular commitment requires a combination of land and sea elements, or land and tactical air elements, or just a land element we can provide this portion by detaching from the single force the strength and type of force required.
We can apply various combinations of this force at home and abroad as the case may warrant. It may be to stop an enemy lodgement on our shores; it may be to assist in UN peace restoring action; it may be to further assist NATO or it may be a combination of these tasks. The point remains, however, that with this type of structure we know what our force is, what it can do, how it can be supported and most important of all, we can give it the required flexibility to meet these changing commitments.
Now, some people have advanced the argument that all this can be done while retaining the three separate services. I suggest to them, however, that it is both dangerous and expensive to retain the separate services. It is dangerous because we have already experienced some of the bitterness of inter-service rivalries. We have seen previous cases where one service will press for particular equipment it feels it must have to carry out a specific function without relating that specific function to over-all defence objectives. We have seen previous cases where a particular service refuses to alter its equipment so that it can carry dual instead of a single function. We have seen previous cases where the purchase of military equipment by the services was made before government policy had been decided on the use of such equipment. In other words-and to this I think we can all agree-there have been times in past years where the three services have procured some types of equipment for themselves without any reference to the needs and requirements of the other services.
In so far as expenditures are concerned, I think that the expense required to maintain the three separate services is both unnecessary and unwarranted. I do not intend to list

Mr. Speaker, the equipment we are procuring combined with the force structure we have created gives us a capability to undertake a variety of tasks anywhere in the world. In cases where we can use our forces for different circumstances, we have insured that our troops will have the proper equipment and fire power to carry out their commitment.
Where we can employ our equipment for different purposes we have built in a dual capability. Thus, for example, our new operational support ships can not only provision the fleet at sea but carry heavy equipment and stores required to support our land forces wherever they may be assigned.

Mr. Speaker, a few moments ago I mentioned unification and I heard again and again in this debate the question "What is meant by unification?" Here is what the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) said about unification, and I quote:

It is quite difficult to determine any clean break between them because there was never intended to be one. Integration is actually the first phase of the total process of unification. Whatever special meaning the word may carry in any given context, in practical terms the process of integration can be but a means to an end and not an end in itself."

In the final analysis, perhaps integration is the wrong word altogether and it is unification of which we should speak-one force with many facets operating at the will of our commands in the fulfilment of our nations defence policy.
I think there can be no mistake that integration and unification are well known and

It is forecast that additional savings due to integration in 1986-67 will not be sufficient to compensate entirely for continuing increased costs including the general military pay increase effective 1 October 1966.
But in all fairness, Mr. Speaker, I think all members will realize that the armed forces like the civilian economy, is suffering from the increase of costs found in any booming economy.
Next, I want to deal with the rumours that we are closing out bases. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Forrestall) raised this point on Monday night and I know that there is great concern in this area and other areas of the country. We have replied to this question, but I would like to bring our reply to the notice of hon. members and to the citizens of the country who are directly affected. We answered as follows:
As was stated in the White Paper 1964, the aim of the reorganization of the Canadian Forces is the achievement of increased efficiency and economy based upon the overall national interest. The proper positioning and grouping of activities and forces, and their amalgamation where practical, is now under study, and it is anticipated that this study will extend over a considerable time. In any event no major bases, including Rivers, will be closed out during 1967. Of course, this does not preclude the possibility of moving units or activities from one base to another. If. and when a decision is taken to close out a specific base the maximum possible advance information will be provided to those who are directly affected.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that I am firmly convinced that we are upholding our governmental responsibility to our armed forces and to the citizens of our country, when dealing with unification.
The force structure that has been created, the projected operational course of deployment planned for the early '70s plus the equipment we are purchasing through our five year $1.5 billion procurement program will enable our armed forces to carry out their duties and responsibilities in support of our national policy.
I am not convinced that we have in any way been secretive about our plans and projections. Canadians have never been more

National Defence Act Amendment aware of our plans concerning our defence policy than they are today. Some people charged that Canadians do not care about defence any more-that it is a dead issue- I do not believe that at all. I believe that Canadians have real knowledge of our defence policy and are secure in the knowledge that what we are doing in the field of defence is good for them and in the best interests of the nation.
Mr. Speaker, we are engaged in a discussions of the principle of unification. I believe the Canadian Armed Forces are anxious to carry out the task of unification.

I agree with the associate minister that this question is important, and I hope he is correct when he expresses the opinion that Canadians generally have a vital interest in it. I should like to see some evidence of that. If it is so, I am delighted. It is important from many points of view, not only because of cost. In this fiscal year we are spending something like $1,575 million on defence. For a country such as Canada with its small population this means an expenditure of something like $75 to $80 for every man, woman and child.
But unification is vitally important from other points of view. It is important not only because of the cost of our defence effort and what we get for our defence dollars but also vitally important because in our course of action we are taking a virtually irreversible step in doing away with the defence set-up that has served us well over the years and substituting another one for it. No matter how unsuitable it may prove to be for Canada

it will be almost impossible effectively to unscramble the situation and get us back to the position we are now in or something like it, regardless of how desirable returning to this situation may be.
I do not want to refer at great length to the associate minister's speech. He talked about things which are true and valid, the desirability of equipping our forces with modern equipment that is versatile, and that sort of thing. That does not necessarily imply that unification, as this bill before us would have it, is necessary to achieve these other desirable ends. In a number of instances the associate minister's reasoning was perfectly correct and valid but in some instances he started with false premises. Naturally, though his reasoning process was correct, he ended with wrong conclusions. He said that this is a time of change, that we have to be adaptable. Nothing could be truer. It does not follow that because you change you make progress. Progress is not automatic. Though you have to change to progress, it does not always follow that by changing you always progress.
When the debate began on this stage of the bill in December the minister spoke for an hour and three quarters. I read his speech carefully. It contains scarcely a statement which cannot be validly challenged. Last evening I saw some remarks reportedly made by the retiring president of the Canadian National, Mr. Donald Gordon. They describe Canada's difficulty at the present time. Mr. Gordon said, "It aint the things you don't know that gets you into trouble, it's the things you know for sure what aint so." In my judgment that is the difficulty with the minister. No matter what authority is quoted, no matter what facts are put forward he simply dismisses them by saying they aint so.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
We could benefit by examining the experience of other countries in this important matter. Having one armed force instead of three is not a new idea. There is nothing new under the sun. Probably dozens of countries have thought of it but in every case have discarded it. In July, 1963, Great Britain produced a white paper entitled "Central Organization for Defence" which in part said:
The object is to improve the central control of defence policy without impairing the efficiency and morale of the fighting services. Their separate identities will be preserved.
The services must preserve their separate identities. In action they are increasingly interdependent. This interdependence must be expected to increase. Nevertheless all experience shows that the fighting spirit of the individual man in battle derives
February 1, 1967	COMMONS
largely from his loyalty to his ship, his unit, or his squadron. The traditions and battle honours of the individual services are a vital factor in morale and fighting efficiency. This must be preserved.
What has been the experience in the United States? Up to quite recent times, until the end of world war II, the United States had only-two departments, a department of the army and a department of the navy. There was also the United States army air corps which in world war II was a very powerful and decisive force but it was not a separate armed service in the sense that we are speaking of now. After world war II the United States examined the whole problem of the administration of its armed forces. The joint chiefs of staff appointed a committee of outstanding army and navy officers in May, 1944, to examine thoroughly three basic systems of defence organization: (1) two departments-war and navy; (2) three departments-war, navy and air; (3) one department-defence. In this connection I quote from a history of the United States air force by Alfred Goldberg, and I should like to emphasize that he is talking about departments, not services.
After ten months of study and travel in every theatre of war, interviews with 52 key military and naval leaders, and one hundred separate meetings in Washington, D.C., the JCS Special Committee, in March 1945, recommended a plan for one department of armed forces consisting of three co-ordinate branches. It advised prompt action to prevent reversion of the air arm to its prewar status and the loss of the gains in efficiency and co-operation made since 1942. The JCS plan included a military commander of the armed forces who would also be chief of staff to the president.
Again quoting from Mr. Goldberg's history:
In response to the president's message, a subcommittee of the Senate committee on military affairs, under Senator Elbert D. Thomas, began working on a unification bill with the representatives of the army and navy-Major General Lauris Norstad and Vice Admiral Arthur W. Radford.
I should mention that what was involved was unification of the departments, not of the services.
Numerous conferences with top leaders of the services followed, and nine separate drafts were prepared. The last draft was introduced as a bill in April 1946 and accepted by the whole committee in May.
This bill became known as the proposed Common Defence Act of 1946, because it provided for a Department of Common Defence comprising three co-ordinate arms. There would be a civilian secretary of common defence, a secretary and a commander for each of the arms, a chief of staff of common defence to rank above all other officers of the armed forces, a council of common defence, a national security resources board, and a central intelligence agency. This bill offered no assurance
National Defence Act Amendment
that the army and navy could retain their special air units.
That bill was not passed. It was withdrawn and another bill known as the National Security Act of 1947 was passed in its place.
The National Security Act of 1947 became law on July 26, 1947. The lawmakers stated their intentions at the beginning of the act in a declaration of policy: to provide a comprehensive program for the future security of the United States; to provide three military departments-the army, the navy (including naval aviation and the marine corps), and the air force-
I shall not quote further, but the interesting point is that in the United States approach the people concerned sought the best advice from the senior officers of their services as to what would be the most efficient and most desirable form for their armed forces to take. They also took the advice of their senior officers with regard to administration of the civilian department. That was in complete contrast to what we see here in Canada. Of course it can be said that Canada's problems are not on all fours with those of the United States or any other country. I would be the first to agree, but nevertheless I think we can learn from the experience of other countries.
It is said that defence policy is an extension of external affairs policy. The white paper published in March, 1964 contains the following at page 6:
In these circumstances, there have developed four parallel methods by which the objectives of Canadian defence policy have been pursued. They are:
(a)	Collective measures for maintenance of peace and security as embodied in the Charter of the United Nations, including the search for balanced and controlled disarmament;
(b)	Collective defence as embodied in the North Atlantic Treaty;
(c)	Partnership with the United States in the defence of North America;
(d)	National measures to discharge responsibility for the security and protection of Canada.
I would like to know if this statement of our objectives is still valid or has there been some undisclosed, subterranean shift in our external affairs policy and therefore a shift in our defence policy which requires a different shape for our armed forces? If this is the case, and if it is the only reason for the proposed re-organization, then the Canadian people have a right to know.
Our forces have been reduced in strength. Many of them are not up to establishment at the present time. In that regard I should like to quote from an editorial in the Charlottetown Guardian of last Monday which in part refers to articles that appeared in the

Under the present faulty command structure, however, it is virtually impossible for the public, parliament, or even the cabinet now to ascertain the true state of affairs. Through firings and early retirements of any seniors who had the courage to speak out, the minister has tended to gather about himself a clique of "yes men". I would agree with this suggestion if we are to retain the type of organization where there is only one channel of communication to the minister. I maintain that the very reverse is true, that when you have a unified force it is only the opinion which results from one set of judgments which will ever come to public notice. If that opinion should prove not to be the best, then the error will be concealed for as long as possible, not through any malicious intent or inefficiency on the part of the commander in chief, the generalissimo, or whatever he might be called, but because human nature is what it is. When there are three separate services with three separate chiefs of staff and suggestions in respect of requirements and demands for equipment and so on are made on behalf of one of the three defence forces, these must stand up to the criticism, the judgments and suggestions which are presented in competition to them.

speechtext:
That is exactly what I am saying. When you have three chiefs of staff you have the best of at least three choices. Under the present situation there is only one type of thinking which will become government policy. I know for a fact that other countries such as Britain have toyed with the monolithic type of structure and have discarded it for that very reason. Where it is used, only one point of view prevails whether or not it is a completely valid point of view. In respect of this defence structure we have what one might refer to as the bed of Procrustes policy of the minister. If a senior officer, no matter how valid his position may be with regard to a policy matter, is a big enough man to stand up and proclaim his position through proper channels to his superiors, he will lose his head if his policy does not fit in with the accepted single policy. This is the practice which has been followed for the past two years.
I have mentioned the fact that on the east coast particularly our navy is under strength. The number of ships at sea and in commission has been seriously reduced. In answer to questions on this point which have been asked over a period of months the minister has replied that this is absolute nonsense. He says that the units which we now have at sea are so much more technically advanced-they have helicopters, variable depth sonar and so on-that eight of them are equal to twice as many of the type in commission four or five years ago. This is true in that limited sense. We must not forget, however, that technical advance among our potential enemies is not stagnating; it is not at a standstill. If one were to project the minister's reasoning beyond a period of a couple of years, perhaps over a few centuries, one would immediately realize that perhaps one world war II frigate would have disposed easily of the Spanish Armada. But that is not the problem we have today. We must keep abreast of developments and have counter-measures for every potential threat that is developed.
In connection with anti-submarine warfare I think it is not fully realized among the general public or the press that there is a new, tremendously important and extremely dangerous dimension to submarine warfare which did not exist in world war II. Up until some time after world war II virtually the only use to which submarines could be put was to attack merchant shipping or naval units. The defence against them was relatively simple. All one had to do was defend the sea lanes. The enemy could not produce any
February 1. 1967	COMMONS
damage without exposing himself to danger. The submarine had to come in close in order to attack. Virtually its only targets were merchant shipping and the naval units protecting that merchant shipping. So it really was a case of keeping the sea lanes open. That type of submarine warfare is still in existence, but it is of only relatively minor importance compared to the tremendous threat which has developed as a result of nuclear-powered submarines armed with nuclear missiles which carry for a very considerable range. They can park anywhere in a huge area of the ocean.
The potential threat to our cities and our communications from these nuclear submarines extends over a wide area. You do not wait for them to come to you. You must search them out. The problem is similar to looking for a needle in a haystack. In my judgment this is of tremendous importance and should not be downgraded. I believe it is the main reason that our naval strength must be kept up to date if we are to be in a position to meet our NATO obligations so far as our naval contribution is concerned.
In this regard there is an apparent conflict in the policy of the government. For the last two years the government has been pretending to have a policy of extending our territorial seas and declaring vast areas, such as the Gulf of St. Lawrence, the bay of Fundy, Hecate strait, Dixon Entrance, and other vast waters, as national waters of Canada. That policy also seems to be in a state of suspended animation or limbo at the present time. If the government pursues that course and the objective is achieved it will then have the additional responsibility of assuring our allies that we are capable of enforcing our sovereignty over those vast areas of water.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
Our allies cannot afford to take the chance that the Gulf of St. Lawrence, for example, might become a sanctuary for potential enemies. Even during world war II it was not possible for us to keep the Gulf of St. Lawrence clear of enemy undersea craft. It will be even more difficult in peacetime to assure our friends and allies that there are not enemy submarines, capable of lobbing atomic missiles into some of the largest population centres of North America, lurking in that area. The minister should assure us that the capability of our navy is such as to be consistent with the implications of the other policy. Let me be perfectly clear by saying that I agree wholeheartedly with the policy of extending our territorial waters, but we must face up to the accompanying responsibilities.

Is it the government's intention to pass on some of our responsibilities for establishing and protecting some of our territory to a friendly neighbour? I raise it again because the fact is we are contributing at the present time to peace keeping forces under the United Nations. If that is going to be a permanent role it should be carried out by a special organization within our armed forces. The effectiveness of our armed forces should not be reduced by gathering up ad hoc peacekeeping units to be shipped off to Cyprus or somewhere else when a special crisis arises.
The training of our armed forces is not particularly suitable for the duties required of peace keeping forces under the United Nations. Consideration should be given in conjunction with other nations to the creation of a special peace keeping force which would be specially trained for the specialized tasks involved. It would have to be a force trained in the diplomatic handling of tense situations. Its members would have to be long suffering and patient in order to be effective under most difficult conditions.
I am very much saddened and sincerely disappointed by the course the minister insists on pursuing. Not long ago we in parliament heard a great long list of legislation that had to be completed, according to the Prime Minister, before the next recess. That list should be culled and legislation of little or no merit should be deleted. Legislative items which the majority of Canadians believe are downright harmful and disadvantageous to the future interests of this country should also be deleted. At the top of the items for deletion I suggest should be the bill presently under discussion.
The policy embodied in the measure before us has all the earmarks of an idea conceived before arguments were gathered to prop it up. It is a tragedy that we should now find ourselves as a nation in the position of embarking upon this policy. I will not be surprised if
February 1, 1967

National Defence Act Amendment the bill passes in the course of time and the minister has his way, but if that turns out to be the case it will be little short of a tragedy for Canada.
One may ask how this could come about. I suppose it came about first because the minister got his way in the cabinet. Apparently for the sake of solidarity his colleagues, some of whom must have great reservations about this matter, went along with the idea. Perhaps the minister might have resigned had they not agreed and a weak government of this kind probably could not afford to have that happen. If I were in their places I should think it better to have the minister as an enemy than as a friend.
The government must have support in the house. No party at the present time particularly wants an election because we have had so many within a few years. It may also be argued that the whole matter of unification is something that is of interest to only those people who are directly concerned and that many many Canadians pretty well ignore it. speechtext:
With the support of the third, fourth and fifth parties, if you like. I do not care what you call them. The fact is that the government at this time represents only a relatively small segment of the Canadian people. Its support is far less than 50 per cent. Under those circumstances the government does not have a mandate to proceed in a bull-headed fashion with highly contentious legislation without first examining that legislation very carefully and without first obtaining the best possible advice available.
For that reason I feel strongly that the subject matter of this bill should have gone to a committee for further study before the house was asked to approve it in principle. The government has no mandate to force its will upon the Canadian people. It is true that it is the largest group in the house and under our system is charged with administration, but it should seek a consensus in respect of highly contentious matters.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
In this regard I have often been disturbed by the interpretation placed on the performance of parliament by our press and other mass media of communication, an interpretation which has found its way into the minds

of the Canadian people. I believe that the workings of parliament are of fundamental importance to our democratic system and that they should be understood. On reading the press of Canada I get the feeling one gets when walking through a hall of mirrors at an exhibition midway. In one place one's image is distorted in one way and in another place in another way. Even if an individual does by chance come across an accurate reflection of what goes on in parliament, there is no way for him to know whether it is distorted or whether it is the actual fact.
I believe that a press which holds the right of freedom of the press in such high esteem, and rightly so, should recognize the very grave responsibilities that go in this day and age with moulding public opinion. The moulding of public opinion should be based on objective observation rather than prejudiced or distorted, pre-conceived views of any situation. All the opposition ask in connection with this very important matter of unification is that it be thoroughly examined, that we have the evidence of witnesses, without prejudice, without trying to force the outcome one way or the other. If unification has the merits the government claims for it, it will stand up under that examination. If it has not, it should not be perpetrated upon the Canadian people.
With regard to what we in the official opposition are trying to do here in parliament I would like to read one quotation and then I shall have concluded my remarks. For convenience I quote from Beauchesne's fourth edition. The passage I shall quote contains quotations from other authorities on the subject of democracy:
In every country attempts have been made to ensure that there shall be some check on the powers of the majority. Lord Bryce said in "Modern Democracies":	"That a majority is always
right, i.e. that every decision it arrives at by voting is wise not even the most fervent democrat has ever maintained seeing that popular government consists in the constant effort of a minority to turn itself by methods of persuasion into a majority which will then reserve the action or modify the decisions of the former majority."
There is a special onus on a minority government when it proceeds on courses that are not reversible. The passage continues:
Decision by majority is not an absolute and unquestionable principle. "Our constitution, to use Burke's phrase, is something more than a problem in arithmetic." There is no divine right of a mere numerical majority any more than or kings. Majority decision is a measure of convenience essential to the dispatch of business, the result, "of a very particular and special convention, confirmed

by long habits of obedience." The idea that a majority, just because it is a majority, is entitled to pass, without full discussion, what legislation it pleases, regardless of the extent of the changes involved or of the intensity of the opposition to them, the idea in fact that majority edicts are the same things as laws, is wholly alien to the spirit of the constitution.
A minority party may question ministers, may criticize but cannot control in the ordinary case a government with a reasonably large majority. There can be no control of the executive where the supporters in parliament are prepared without question to obey the leaders of their party-through the whips. All that the minority party-the opposition-can do without support from members of the majority party is to question, inquire and criticize, but whilst this does not amount to control it is an important method of checking abuses of power. With the support of a majority-
I contend that the government is abusing its imagined power in this situation.
-of members it would be possible for a cabinet to suspend the sitting of parliament, have the minority members arrested, withdraw the safeguards of liberty such as habeas corpus and freedom of speech, and to establish virtually a dictatorship. All this, too, could be done within the law. It is surprising how few members of the general public appreciate how uncontrolled the cabinet is where it has the support of a loyal majority in parliament and that ''the supremacy of parliament" in this sense is absolute and subject to no real safeguards of any kind.
We may add that the majority of the House of Commons does not always represent the majority of the electors in the country. It often happens that, owing to the redistribution of electoral districts, a party may come out of the general elections with a majority of elected members without having received the majority of the votes given by the electors who went to the polls or whose names are on the electoral lists. That party may form a cabinet, but the official opposition together with other anti-ministerial groups, though sitting to the Sneaker's left, are the real representatives of the people: and their right to challenge bv legitimate means every measure or proceeding sponsored bv ministers cannot be disnuted. In respect of this legislation I believe that the government represents a minoritv, and a small minority, of the people of Canada. Therefore it is my intention to vote against second reading.
