speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, implicit in the decision that this house is called on to make on second reading of this bill is much more than simply questions of organization, machinery, uniforms or ranks, important though these may be. The basic question posed by approval in principle of this bill is the whole question of the future role of Canada's armed forces, the purpose
National Defence Act Amendment and function which they are to serve and the contribution in the sphere of defence that Canada can best make to the security of the people of this country and of the world. Viewed in this light, I have come to the conclusion, somewhat reluctantly I must say, that I must support this bill on second reading. I say reluctantly because I resent, with others, the obstinacy with which the minister and the government have refused to do what it seems to me common sense and courtesy both require, that is, send the bill before second reading to the defence committee.
Many distinguished officers and others who have served this country have expressed serious apprehensions about unification. Why could they not have been allowed to present their views before the committee and the public in that way before we are asked to approve in principle this legislation? Another reason I am supporting the bill with reluctance is that it might seem to be support of the defence policy of this government as enunciated in the white paper and reiterated by the minister in his speech in this debate on December 7 last. I have very serious differences with the policy of the government. I find the defence policy of this government evasive, inadequate, ambiguous and unresponsive to the challenging opportunities that Canada's special position makes possible.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
I am reluctant because I have found, in one edition at any rate, that in the 65 pages of the minister's speech the reasons for unification given by the minister were uninspiring and non-persuasive. As the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) pointed out, there was no explanation whatsoever of the future role of the Canadian forces which would justify the inevitable dislocations involved in unification. The minister has put the cart before the horse. He has told us that he will change completely the structure of the Canadian armed services before telling us what the function and role of those services are to be. In the 65 pages of his speech I find only two paragraphs referring to Canada's policy, and they are a reiteration of the policy in the white paper on defence. I remind the house that this policy consisted of a standpat acceptance of the obligations, regardless of whether they are dated or outdated, that had been assumed in the NATO alliance, and a complete failure to judge whether they were appropriate or obsolete at that particular time. This is still the policy that is put before us. However, if the appropriate question is
February 1, 1967

National Defence Act Amendment asked and the right answer given, then I think this answer justifies unification as the most appropriate and suitable way of performing the role which we consider to be the effectve and proper role for Canada.
What are the present roles of our armed services? Roughly speaking there are five or six. As is well known we provide, integrated with the forces of our NATO alliance, an army brigade in Germany and an air division which is either wholly in Germany or shortly to be moved there. We have our share of the North Atlantic anti-submarine defences. In NORAD we participate in the air defence of North America. We contribute peace keeping forces in a number of theatres under the aegis of the United Nations. We have a mobile command at St. Hubert.
It is our view that we should now abandon some of these roles. We should withdraw our brigade and air division from Europe. We should close down the totally obsolete and useless Bomarc SAGE air defences against a non-existent bomber threat. We should review our anti-submarine role. We should concentrate on a tri-service or unified, lightly armed, highly mobile force available for peace keeping and other intervention roles. We should provide the fire extinguisher which would help put out fires which might spread into major conflagrations. To use the modern jargon, we should be ready to put out the fires which might escalate into a nuclear holocaust.
If, as the present government asserts and reasserts continually, we are to continue our present roles in which different services perform isolated and different activities, then I think unification makes no sense at all, or at least it is not worth, the trouble that is involved. But if we contemplate joint operations in which the services combine in the operations, then unification becomes desirable if not imperative.
My criticism of the government is that it has failed to make a clearcut decision and therefore has failed to present what would be a compelling argument for unification. I say we should withdraw our brigade and air division from Europe. Why do I say so? I do not think it is good enough merely to make such a proposal without supplying the reasons for it. There are at least four reasons for withdrawing our brigade. Our brigade is armed with Honest John rockets or tactical weapons. It is stationed in the forward zone in Germany. It forms a small, although highly efficient, part of or contribution to NATO

strategy, the strategy of confronting a possible U.S.S.R. all-out attack on western Europe with tactical nuclear weapons.
This proposal was orginally made in 1954 and adopted in 1958. In our view it has become obsolete now and indeed provocative. I cannot go into all the reasons for this but I just want to say that one of the reasons is that both sides now have these tactical weapons the use of which would be so destructive as to be insane, and I do not think this word is too strong. General Ailleret, the French chief of staff, had this to say in the Novem-ber-December issue of Survival, a publication of the Institute of Strategic Studies in Great Britain:
It is clear that even a purely tactical nuclear exchange would wipe out Europe over a depth of 1,800 miles from the Atlantic to the Soviet frontier.
I ask the following question: What have we Canadians to do with potential involvement in this suicidal madness if it were ever to come about?
Defence Secretary McNamara has given additional information on this question. He said:
Thousands of U.S. warheads deployed on the continent for the immediate defence of Europe have a combined explosive strength of more than 10,000 times the force of the atomic bombs exploded at Hiroshima and Nagasaki.
He left no doubt whatever-and I remind the minister of this because at one time he was not too clear about it-that this tactical nuclear force represented a substantial preponderance over similar Russian weapons but not a monopoly.
The threat of a deliberate all-out invasion or the use of this massive concentration of power in Europe is at the very lowest end of the spectrum of possibilities, if I may use an expression which is used in this sort of discussion. Indeed, no sane person would launch intentionally such a cataclysm. But as long as this confrontation exists the escalation of threats and bluffs might precipitate a disaster. What is needed is that this massive confrontation be thinned out and eventually dissolved. It makes no sense at all.
Even if I am wrong about this, the need for a Canadian contribution is non-existent. General Foulkes informed the defence committee a year or so ago that as long ago as 1960 the military leaders of NATO approved of Canadian withdrawal from the front line into the position of a mobile reserve. He told us in the committee that this difficult situation, namely, the problem of supplies for the
February 1, 1967

Canadian brigade, was appreciated by the NATO authorities in 1960 and in view of the build-up of the German army to 12 divisions, the supreme allied commander, General Norstad, agreed to place the brigade group in mobile reserve and allow the German forces to take over this forward task on the east German border. This proposal was agreed to on the military level in the early 1960's but, perhaps for political reasons, it has not been implemented.
Then General Foulkes, after going on to point out that it cost about three times as much to maintain a Canadian brigade-indeed, for the price we pay a corps of two divisions could be maintained-asked whether this makes NATO sense? He replied in this way:
It was originally intended that as the European partners increased in economic and military strength, the North American forces would be brought home and provide a strategic reserve. This trend toward the Europeans taking over their own territorial defence is both militarily and economically sound and providing there are no serious political difficulties the change-over should be accomplished before the end of the decade.
I rely on the words of General Foulkes because I think they make common sense. There is no military reason whatever for maintaining our forces there. It has been suggested that there may be a continuing political reason and indeed in the white paper the so-called political reasons are the only ones that are advanced for the maintenance of this excessive commitment. The only political reason that I have ever heard is that the Canadian withdrawal would rock the NATO boat-a phrase used to justify from time to time a certain immobility by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin). It is also said that it would persuade the United States, whose forces in Europe may perhaps constitute a stabilizing factor, to withdraw its troops.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
I suggest this is nonsense. The United States is quite capable of deciding its own role without undue influence resulting from the fact that Canada, for its own good reasons, has decided to withdraw its brigade and air division from Europe. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, all the political arguments point exactly the opposite way. The cold war and the massive military confrontation in Europe have become an anachronism of which Europeans themselves, as anyone who has been to Europe knows, are heartily sick. The danger that the red army will engulf western
National Defence Act Amendment Europe and, by the parity of reasoning on the other side, the danger that the armies of NATO will seek to roll back the frontiers of the Warsaw Pact, are equally unreal. If both NATO and the Warsaw Pact are incapable of being used to liquidate the cold war and improve east-west relations they will have to be scrapped. They no longer correspond to political realities. The centre of gravity of the threats to world peace will be in Asia and Africa, not in central Europe. Our government's continued adherence to obsolete NATO strategy is a symbol of its lack of independence and initiative.
What I have said about our brigade applies with even greater force to our vulnerable air division which, because of its vulnerability to Russian rockets, would in moments of tension constitute a positive danger of provocation to hasty first strike action on one side or the other. Here again, my authority for this statement is General Foulkes. Perhaps I have not the time and should not get into an elaboration of that statement, but the fact remains that if you have a highly vulnerable, highly dangerous strike force, in a moment of danger the desire to hit first is so powerful that the weapons themselves constitute a provocation and a source of danger.
This role was described a long time ago by a military commentator, Mr. John Gellner, who I think supports and sometimes I believe advises this government, as a costly $500 million mistake. I think the only thing wrong with calling it a $500 million mistake is that is much too low a figure. A great deal more than that is involved at this time.
I ask this question: Why is it, after four years in office, this government has failed to liquidate or discontinue these expensive mistakes, these dangerous commitments or, apparently, to do a single thing about them? The minister himself spoke in criticism of these roles before he assumed the position he has today. Is the failure to act the result of timidity or fear of upsetting some of our allies? What is it that compels us to maintain at considerable expense, and quite inconsistently with the policy of unification now advanced by the minister, these particular roles?
These are negative arguments, Mr. Speaker. The principal argument for Canada's concentration on a highly mobile reserve is that it could make a positive contribution to future peace. With our limited resources we cannot do everything. Indeed we should not, as now, try to do a little of everything. The hon.
February 1, 19G7

National Defence Act Amendment member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) and the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) suggested that peace keeping through the United Nations is not exactly popular at the United Nations these days. It is well known that there are difficulties about financing and indeed difficulties in the operations themselves.
But I suggest that those operations in which Canada has taken part, in the Middle East, Cyprus and in the Congo, have played a vital role in preventing the spread of wars which could have been dangerous. In terms of effort, time and money they have been infinitely worth while. There were difficulties when these operations were launched and they were launched and improvised, if you will, because circumstances demanded that they be launched.
I see the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Macdonald), the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I know he worked hard to secure United Nations approval of our idea about how the peace keeping forces should be organized, but so far this has not been possible. I suggest that when emergencies arise again those emergencies will create solutions. It is vitally important to peace that we have available throughout the world, and Canada is in a very good position to contribute, forces that will be able to step in when emergencies arise.
If, Mr. Speaker, the rule of law is ever to prevail in an unstable world, and I think it will, then peace keeping forces will and must have increasing importance in the future. We are now discussing Viet Nam and the crisis in Rhodesia. If there is a settlement in Viet Nam, and let us hope to God there will be a settlement fairly soon, there will be need for a police force to see that the settlement is effectively carried out. The same situation might arise if sanctions are effective in Rhodesia. I am quite certain that during the course of history there will be a call again and again for the fire extinguisher, a call for the type of lightly armed force that this country is in a position to provide.
Of course the mobile force we propose, and upon which we think we should concentrate, would not be confined to operations under the aegis of the United Nations. I recall that when we were at NATO the military authorities told us about possible danger to NATO's flanks, so it may be vitally important to have a mobile reserve that could get there in good time. This sort of contribution might turn out
[Mr. Brewin.l
to be far more important than the massive, tactical nuclear confrontation in central Europe.
In this connection I recall to the house the words of Wayland Young. I believe that like many other British people he has become a peer with a new name, but that was his name. He issued a pamphlet entitled, "The Bomb and Politics", and this is what he said:
It was lightly armed common sense which saved the day in those places (East Africa, Malaysia, Cyprus); cheap, tough, portable weapons and above all mobility. The first rule in this sort of operation is, if you get there first, you do not have to shoot.
It is my submission, Mr. Speaker, that this concept of Canada's role fits in with Canada's special position and aptitudes. It happens to be a fact that we do not have to be absorbed, as some other nations are, with fears of direct attack on the soil of Canada. This is a traditional approach, but it happens that Canada does not have to be preoccupied with that. The facts of life are, whether or not necessarily by choice, that our neighbours are the most powerful military nation in the world. It is unthinkable that the United States would permit any hostile forces to establish themselves on Canadian territory without massive resistance. It is, therefore, unthinkable that any hostile nation, if such there be, would risk retaliation.
I hasten to add that this does not mean, of course, that the mobile force which would be created would be of no value in the defence of Canada or that we do not have to carry out the surveillance of Canadian territory. Of course we do. It does not mean either that we should do as some people say we can do since we are protected by the United States, namely, that we can be either neutral or passive or do nothing about our responsibility for defence. What it does mean, I suggest, is that we are freer than some other nations by reason of this fact to contribute to what in today's nuclear world should be the supreme objective, the prevention of wars and the limitation of wars if they break out.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
No one wins a war in this world today. What we must direct our efforts to is to finding the most efficient instruments (a) to prevent and (b) to limit wars, if they occur. I suggest that a unified force of the type we have discussed would be a useful instrument in that regard.
It sometimes seems to me that we are deluded today by the efficacy of massive, unusable power. Our task is to see that usable
February 1. 1967	COMMONS
power is available where it is needed to create stability in an unstable world. In this field Canada can for the first time, if we have the imagination to do so, escape from a role in defence which is purely subsidiary either to the imperial strategy of Britain, though at a certain stage in history this was quite naturally what we depended upon, or to the great power strategy of the United States of America. In this proposal of a unified Canadian force lies the possibility of making for the first time a distinctively Canadian contribution.
I suggest that in our centennial year it would be quite fitting, Mr. Speaker, to see the emergence of a distinctively Canadian contribution to world security, one most fitted to the circumstances. This would be more valuable to our allies than what we are doing at the present time in the matter of defence, though that we do it efficiently I have no doubt at all. It is because we in this party-and I think I speak for the other members in this party-see in the unification of the armed services a contributing factor to this goal that we propose to support the bill.
I believe that if the minister and the government of the day would only put the problem in this light they would secure the loyalty, even the enthusiasm, of many men and women in Canada. I cannot say, as did the last speaker, that they would have the support of the majority of them, but I certainly think they would secure the support and enthusiasm of our armed services. Changes cannot be made without creating opposition. But when making changes, Mr. Speaker, we should quite frankly and openly declare why they are needed, that in this case what is being proposed is in accordance with a new concept fitted to the nuclear world of the sixties.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, this is a particular contribution Canada can make to the world today. But so far the minister and the government have failed to make this declaration and in not doing so I think have damaged the cause of unification rather than helped it. Because this is what we believe, and subject to what we may be advised in the defence committee and during the future deliberations on this matter, I feel reluctantly obliged to say, for the reasons I have already given, that we will support this bill on second reading.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I approach this subject from a somewhat different angle than most members who have taken part so far, mainly because
National Defence Act Amendment of the interest I have had for some time in international affairs. It has always been a belief of mine that defence policy is nothing more nor less than a function of foreign affairs and is part of the foreign policy of the country involved.
It has been somewhat distressing in listening to and reading the debate to see the line which has been taken by Her Majesty's loyal opposition. In this instance the action of the Conservative party reminds me of King Canute, who called for his chair, sat it down at the tide line, put up his hand and ordered the tide to go back. Well, Mr. Speaker, the tide did not and neither will this bill. The Conservatives have still not changed from the time of the middle period of last century when in Great Britain the Conservative party there attempted to stop the Libera] government of Mr. Gladstone from preventing the purchase of commissions in the Queen's army. They failed at that time too.
Many arguments have been raised against unification, Mr. Speaker, and one of the silliest and least logical, it seems to me, is that which insists that people will fight only for the sake of a regiment. I should like to quote from Douglas MacArthur's "Reminiscences", the paperback edition. At page 470 he is describing why a man fights for his country and why he risks his life. He says:
These men will suffer hunger and thirst, broiling suns and frozen reaches, but they must go on and on and on when everything within them seems to stop and die. They will grow old in youth burned out in searing minutes, even though life owes them many tranquil years. In these troublesome times of confused and bewildered international sophistication, let no man misunderstand why they do that which they must do. These men will fight, and, perchance die, for one reason only-for their country-
They will fight for their country, Mr. Speaker, not for their regiment. I think it is incumbent upon us as parliamentarians to give our men, who may be called upon to risk their lives, the necessary tools to do the job. We cannot have armed forces in the twentieth century, fighting on the basis of what was suitable for war during the late nineteenth century, using weapons which were almost obsolete at the end of the first world war.
Other arguments have been raised against this bill, Mr. Speaker, and one of them is that a great many officers have left the services. And I am not surprised. Whenever a new defence policy is introduced and someone does not agree with it I believe he should leave the services and if he wishes to oppose
February 1, 1967

National Defence Act Amendment the policy he should do so from outside the service. I think that those members of the armed forces who have taken that tack are to be congratulated on their honesty. At the same time 1 do not regard their departure as that much of a loss. A great many younger men have been kept back because of these people who have served long and honourably but whose concepts of what the world is like are perhaps outmoded and it is time for them to be replaced. It is much better both for the government and for the minister that these people depart.
I recall the time when the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) was prime minister and used to complain bitterly that his government was ineffective not because his ministers were ineffective but because there were too many Liberal senior civil servants. If the leader of the government at that time really thought that was so he should have fired them because they were old government employees and some of them were Privy Council appointees. I have no objection to seeing these senior officers depart for greener fields, as they see it; similarly, I have no objection to their fighting for what they believe.
Having read all the speeches and listened to a great many of them, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the basis and justification for unification in our particular circumstances lie in what we are able to do in foreign affairs. As I said, defence policy is a function of foreign policy and our armed forces can only be considered in relationship to it. It is not a matter of isolating the services and looking upon them as something to play around with, putting men in pretty uniforms and marching them up and down the House of Commons lawns. I have always regarded the navy, the army and the air force as a waste, a drain, an expenditure of money we could use in other areas much more profitably.
Therefore, it seems to me that there are certain legitimate conclusions that flow from that attitude. Our foreign policy has been oriented toward joint action with other countries, and for obvious reasons. We have concentrated on the United Nations, with NATO becoming less and less an effective force in the world, its usefulness declining steadily. One of the reasons for this is that the tensions between the United States and Russia have declined. That is also why the present Prime Minister insists in implementing article II of the NATO treaty.

[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
Since our attention is directed to the United Nations, it is necessary to define what role we can play in its operations. To date we have participated in several exercises with the United Nations which have served a useful purpose. In operations of this sort the United Nations has been able to exercise influence, sometimes decisive, in preventing brush fires from growing into greater fires. This is a very useful and very necessary service in our world. In addition, as the United Nations moves away from dominance by the two great powers, the United States and Russia, and begins to acquire a life of its own, effective opportunities for United Nations intervention in brush-fire areas will become more important. If Canada is to play a useful role we must provide ourselves with the tools to be effective in these activities.
I have always believed that we shall have many of these brush-fire wars because the world is not politically sophisticated. Politicians have not worked out effective means of avoiding direct confrontations. They search desperately for face-saving measures to dig themselves out of the holes in which they inadvertently find themselves. We are always trying to save face. A peace keeping force in this area can also be very effective. As we become more sophisticated, as the developing countries become more sophisticated, I hope it will become less and less necessary for the United Nations to intervene. In the meantime Canada can make a most useful contribution in this area, especially if we are prepared to lead. Under the present government I believe we have given notable leadership.
Other implications must be drawn from the fact that no matter how much we want to we shall never be able to defend ourselves from our neighbouring nations, Russia and the United States. We border these countries and sometimes it is difficult to say which is the more dangerous, the United States with its economic invasion or Russia with the threat of physical invasion. At present we are at peace with both these nations and we hope that this continues. If either one decided to attack us we could not defend ourselves. We have too much land and too few defence resources.
The former government entered into an agreement with the United States whereby we gave up responsibility for defending ourselves to the United States in return for a small participation in the defence structure. The impact of this has been to extend the United States border to our northern border.
February 1. 1967	COMMONS
We are allowed to play a small role. We were allowed to buy certain weapons which had to have nuclear warheads. Unfortunately the government of the day bought the bombs but neglected to buy the warheads and we were saddled with much expense without any effective way of making these weapons efficient. I am not sure of this but I understand that the weapons had no explosive power and that in some instances sand was used as ballast. Had we been attacked we would have fired these bombs hoping the invaders would be smothered in sand.
As Canada is a peace-loving country, and I hope it is, we do not need an army for aggression. As we have common borders with the two super powers we are very likely to be the battleground in any conflict between them. We need a defensive army to look after ourselves, if we need anything. As I understand it, we are on the way to giving up our nuclear capacity. As our weapons would not be much of a deterrent to these two super powers, there will be small loss.
It seems that this leads us back to unification or integration of our forces as a reasonable method of ensuring that we have the power to play the role we want to play in external affairs. Unification or integration -call it what you will-is a reasonable, logical concept if one accepts the assumptions on which it is based.
I would not wish to repeat the opinions of former generals read into the record the other day by the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson). All these generals wrote memoirs after the second world war and they unanimously agreed that the old method of carry-
Business of the House ing on war with divided commands was inefficient, ineffective, and cost a great many of their soldiers' lives. One of my hobbies happens to be reading the memoirs of generals, not necessarily for edification but for enjoyment. I enjoy the way war is depicted in books, the way Eisenhower criticizes Montgomery, Montgomery criticizes Bradley and on and on. All these comments of the generals show one thing, that the old system has to go, that it is no longer efficient and something needs to be evolved. May I call it six o'clock.

subtopic: AGREEMENT OF SENATE TO CONSIDERATION OF PENSIONS OF RETIRED CIVIL SERVANTS BY JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: I have the honour to inform the house that a message has been received from the Senate informing this house that the Senate do agree that the Special Joint Committee of the Senate and House of Commons on the Public Service of Canada be empowered to inquire into and report upon the matter of the pensions paid to retired civil servants or their dependants under the provisions of the Public Service Superannuation Act.
